title: Six decisions before anyone spoke: setting, role, and consent

objectives.statement: Trace a named fact in a fictional clinical record back to the specific setup decision that made it available, and state what the record would have contained instead under a stated alternative arrangement.

Distinguish a negotiated and revisable agreement from a recorded permission, state what has to be disclosed for the agreement to mean anything including the limits the person does not control, and identify the point at which such an agreement changed.

Classify who holds which role in a described encounter and decide which acts a person in a non-clinical role may and may not perform, justifying each decision from the act and the person it lands on instead of from the subject matter.

Prepare an accessible simulated encounter by settling its place and privacy, who is present and on what basis, each person's role and the purpose, the time available, the record and who reads it, and the communication arrangements, and state the resulting agreement and its limits.

scenes.title: The sentence that is only there because someone asked
scenes.contentHtml:
The sentence that is only there because someone asked

R. is 34, works rotating night shifts in a warehouse, and was referred by a general practitioner to a community mental-health clinic. R. is invented for this course, and every detail here and in the lessons around it was written for teaching. Nothing describes a real person.

The record of R.'s first appointment runs to about a page. One line near the end says that R. has had passive thoughts that life is not worth the effort, with no plan, no intent, and nothing done. R. did not raise it. It is in the record because a direct question was asked forty minutes in, after the medical student had left the room, and after R. had been told what would and would not go into the letter back to the GP.

Four arrangements stand behind that one line: how long the appointment was, who was in the room, what the appointment was for and therefore which questions belonged in it, and what R. had been told about the record. None of the four is a fact about R. All four changed what is now known about R.

That is the subject of this lesson. Someone arranges the conditions under which a person can speak before anyone describes what the person said. The arrangements are part of the clinical material, and an account that leaves them out cannot explain why some things are in it and other things are not. The next scene sets out the full list of six.

People leave things out, and they can say what they were avoiding

Two large United States survey samples asked adults whether they had ever withheld information from a clinician. Among respondents who reported experiencing depression, suicidal thoughts, abuse, or sexual assault, 47.5% in one sample and 40.0% in the other said they had kept at least one of those from a clinician. The reasons endorsed most often were being embarrassed, not wanting to be judged or lectured, not wanting to be pushed into follow-up they did not want, and not wanting the information in their medical record. That last reason was named by 57.1% and 52.7% of them.

Those are self-reports from online survey panels, not observed encounters, and they carry all the recall and selection problems that go with the method. What they establish is narrower than a prevalence figure and more useful: people who withhold can name what they were avoiding, and more than half of them named the written record among their reasons. The record is something a clinician decides how to describe at the start of a conversation. It is one of the arrangements.

The other common fear belongs to the person asking rather than the person answering, and it is worth naming early because it decides whether the question in R.'s notes gets asked at all. In a two-year study, 170 adolescents who had been discharged from psychiatric hospital were asked about suicidal thoughts repeatedly, and being asked more often was not followed by higher scores; more than half the group scored lower at the end than at the start. That is one study, in adolescents, in continuing treatment, with no control group, so it cannot show that asking helps. It is evidence against a specific worry: that raising the subject plants the thought.

Put the two together and R.'s silence until asked stops looking like a fact about R.'s character. It is a property of an arrangement in which nobody had asked yet.

Check
id check-description-inference-carryover

Before reading on, sort these four statements about R.'s appointment into what a listener observed, what R. reported, and what a listener added. Write one line each.

  1. R. said the thoughts come mostly on the drive home.
  2. The appointment ran 50 minutes.
  3. R. answered the direct question without hesitating.
  4. R. found the question a relief.

Then say which of the four you would be least willing to write in a record, and why.

Items 2 and 3 are things a person in the room could observe, though 3 already contains a judgement about what counts as hesitating. Item 1 is R.'s report, and it stays R.'s report however plausible it sounds. Item 4 is an addition: nobody has said it, and the only evidence for it is that the answer came easily. The one you should be least willing to write is 4, because writing it turns a listener's impression into a line in a document that R. and other clinicians will later read as though it came from R.

That sorting is the work of the preceding outcome, Description, inference, and interpretation. This lesson depends on it and does not repeat it. If the four items were hard to separate, the recovery route at the end of the practice scene gives a way back in that does not require the earlier lesson.

What this lesson does, and what it leaves to other lessons

By the end you should be able to do four things.

  • Trace a named fact in R.'s account back to the specific setup decision that made it available, and say what would have been different under a stated alternative.
  • Distinguish an agreement that was negotiated and can be revisited from a signature on a form, and state what has to be disclosed for the agreement to mean anything, including the parts the person cannot control.
  • Say, for a described encounter, who holds which role and which acts a person in a non-clinical role may and may not perform, justifying the answer from the act and not from the subject matter.
  • Prepare a simulated encounter yourself: settle where it happens and who can hear, who is present and on what basis, who each person is and what the conversation is for, how long there is, what will be written and who reads it, and what has to be arranged for the person to take part at all. Then say what the person has agreed to, and what the limits of that agreement are.

Three things are deliberately absent. This lesson does not describe R.'s mental state, which is the mental-status observation outcome later in this module. It does not ask what might be going on with R. or weigh the possibilities, which the mood outcomes take up further along. And it does not teach how questions are put once the conversation has started, which is open and focused inquiry, the outcome directly after this one.

Callout
id callout-teaching-boundary-orientation

Teaching example, not medical advice. R., the clinic, the student, the appointment, and every quoted line are invented for this course. You are reading a record of a conversation you did not conduct and are not authorised to conduct. Studying how an encounter was arranged does not authorise you to arrange one with a real person, and nothing in this lesson is a basis for any decision about anyone's care.

The withholding figures come from two national United States survey samples that asked about the same list of imminent threats; they describe what respondents said about themselves and cannot show what happened in any consultation. The evidence that repeated asking was not followed by increases in suicidal thinking comes from a single two-year study of 170 adolescents already in psychiatric treatment, which its authors describe as uncontrolled and unable to establish a mechanism. Neither source supports a rule about how or when to ask any real person about suicide, and this lesson gives none.

scenes.title: Six decisions, made before R. said anything
scenes.contentHtml:
Six decisions, made before R. said anything

Someone made six decisions about R.'s appointment. Most were settled before R. arrived, and one was put to R. in the waiting area about thirty seconds before it started. Each has a consequence you can find in the record.

Definition
id definition-settinglabel Setting

The setting is the arranged conditions of an encounter: the place, the people present, the time available, the way information will be recorded and shared, and what each person is there to do. It is chosen, so it can be chosen differently, and it constrains what a person is able to say.

1. Place: who could hear

R.'s appointment happened in a consulting room with a door that shut and a window onto a corridor. The blind was down. A colleague knocked once at minute 22 and was waved away.

The knock is the consequence. R. stopped mid-sentence, and the sentence did not resume in the same form. Nobody recorded what was lost, because a thing that was not said leaves no trace.

Auditory privacy is a property of the building and of how the service runs, and it is not always available. A review of privacy in emergency medicine notes that curtains give visual separation while leaving conversations audible, and that overheard conversation between staff is a routine way confidentiality is compromised without anyone intending it. The point for R.'s clinic is not that the room was adequate. It is that whether the room was adequate is a question with an answer, and someone should have asked it before the appointment instead of after the knock.

2. People: who else was there, and on what basis

A final-year medical student sat in for the first 25 minutes. R. was asked in the waiting area whether that was acceptable and said yes. R.'s partner, who drove R. there, waited in the car.

Two things about that arrangement are worth separating. The first is whether R. was asked at all. In a survey at a Portuguese university hospital, 185 psychiatry patients were asked about their experience of medical students in their care. Of those who recalled the encounter, 75% said the doctor had asked whether they minded the students being present, and 31% said the students had introduced themselves as medical students and asked permission themselves. Some respondents reported that a student's presence made it harder to talk about an intimate problem. The gap between those two figures is the interesting part: being asked about a student and knowing who the student is are different pieces of information, and patients received the first far more often than the second.

The second thing is contested, and this lesson does not settle it. A United States emergency-medicine review from 2006 records both readings of the question: many institutions treat the general consent signed at admission as covering a student observer, and other writers hold that explicit consent should be sought for each observation. The same review states that visitors should be present only with the patient's permission. Which reading governs depends on the institution and the jurisdiction, and a 2006 source cannot tell you what any current policy says.

R.'s clinic used the second reading, asked, and got a yes. That yes was later revised, which is the subject of the next scene.

3. Role: who each person was, and what each was there to do

The student was introduced by name and as a medical student. The clinician said what the appointment was for, in one sentence, before anything else: to understand what had been happening over the past few months and to work out together what might help.

Definition
id definition-role-claritylabel Role clarity

Role clarity means every person in an encounter knows who the others are, what each is there to do, and which of them carries responsibility for any decision that follows. It is a property of what was said out loud, not of what was true.

Role clarity is not politeness. It determines what a person's agreement is agreement to. Canadian guidance on consent to psychiatric treatment states that the identity of the person who will provide the treatment is part of what has to be disclosed, and that delegating the consent discussion to a different clinician risks missing concerns that matter to the person's decision. Someone who agrees to talk to a doctor has not thereby agreed to talk to a student, and someone who agrees to an assessment has not agreed to a treatment.

That has a direct consequence for you. You are reading this material the way the student sat through the first 25 minutes, and with less standing than she had: present at it, and authorised to act on none of it. The line does not run between easy topics and difficult ones. It runs between acts.

Act Where it sits Why
Reading R.'s record and saying which arrangements produced which facts Study The object is a fictional record. Being wrong changes an argument.
Asking a real person a direct question about suicidal thoughts because this lesson showed one being asked Outside The object is a person, and the act commits whoever asks to what happens next.
Rewriting a badly arranged fictional encounter into a better one Study The output is an argument about arrangements, inspectable and revisable.
Telling a real acquaintance what a clinic would or would not put in their letter Outside It is a statement about a service's actual practice and law, made without standing to know either.

Notice that the topic is identical down the column. Every row is about suicide, records, and clinics. What moves an act across the line is who it lands on and what follows from getting it wrong.

4. Time: how much there was, and when

R.'s appointment was booked for 50 minutes at 4pm. R. had finished a night shift at 6am, slept badly, and asked twice how long this would take, because the next shift started at 10pm.

Fifty minutes is a choice a service made, and services choose very differently. A systematic review of 179 studies covering more than 28 million consultations in 67 countries found average primary-care consultation length ranging from 48 seconds in Bangladesh to 22.5 minutes in Sweden, with 18 countries containing about half the world's population at five minutes or less. Those are averages across whole health systems, from published data up to 2016, and none of them is a psychiatric assessment. They are enough to make one thing clear: an account of interviewing that assumes an hour is describing one kind of service, and the person reading it may work somewhere the number is five.

Time changes the order of a conversation, and the order changes what gets reached. In R.'s appointment the alcohol question came at minute 34 and the direct question about suicidal thoughts at minute 40. Either could have been the thing that did not fit.

5. Record: what would be written, and who would read it

Before the history began, the clinician said three things: a letter would go to R.'s GP, R. could read it, and R. could ask for anything in it to be discussed first.

Whether the clinician can promise that everything stays between them is a separate question, with an answer that depends on where the clinic is. In the United States, statutory duties to warn or protect a third party after a threat differ state by state: one review counts roughly 27 to 33 states with mandatory duties, 9 to 11 with permissive ones, and 6 to 13 with no statute, the ranges reflecting disagreement about how particular statutes should be classified. Other countries organise the question through professional regulation or general law instead. A clinician is expected to know the rule where they practise.

Definition
id definition-confidentialitylabel Confidentiality

Confidentiality is the duty to keep what a person discloses within the care of the people who need it for that person's care. It is strong and it is not absolute. Its limits are set by the law and professional regulation of a particular place, which is why a description of them is only accurate for one jurisdiction at a time.

Saying this at the start rather than at the moment it becomes relevant is a setup decision with a cost and a benefit. The cost is that it introduces a caution into a conversation before there is anything to be cautious about. The benefit is that anything R. says afterwards was said knowing it.

6. Communication access: whether the conversation is possible at all

R. speaks the clinician's language, so nothing was arranged. That is itself a decision, and it is the one most often made by not thinking about it.

Definition
id definition-communication-accesslabel Communication access

Communication access covers the arrangements that make an encounter usable by the person in it: a professional interpreter, a signed-language interpreter, longer appointments, written summaries, a hearing loop, an easy-read explanation, or a communication partner. It is arranged before the encounter, because it cannot be improvised inside it.

A systematic review of 28 studies found that professional interpreters were associated with fewer communication errors and better comprehension, service use, clinical outcomes, and satisfaction than ad hoc interpreters, meaning family members, accompanying friends, or untrained bilingual staff. Most of those studies were observational and carried out in the United States, so the review reports an association across a varied literature and not the result of a trial. The practical reading is narrow and firm enough to act on: the person who came with the patient is not the arrangement, and using them as one degrades what the encounter can produce.

Had R. needed an interpreter and the clinic used the partner waiting in the car, the passive thoughts would probably not be in the record, and the reason would have nothing to do with R.

scenes.title: What R. actually agreed to, and when it changed
scenes.contentHtml:
What R. actually agreed to, and when it changed

Nothing in R.'s appointment was signed. The agreement was made in speech, across five exchanges, and it was different at the end from what it had been at the start. Here is the whole of it, reconstructed from the record. Every line is invented for teaching.

Waiting area, before the appointment. Receptionist: "There's a medical student sitting in this afternoon. Is that all right?" R., standing, coat on, student two metres away: "Yeah, that's fine."

Minute 0. Clinician: "I'm a psychiatrist here. This is a final-year medical student, sitting in to learn. What I want to do in the next fifty minutes is understand what's been going on since the spring and work out with you what might help. I'll write to your GP afterwards. You can read that letter, and if there's anything in it you'd rather we talked about first, say so and we will. Some of what I ask will be personal. You can decline any question and it doesn't stop the rest."

Minute 24. R.: "Can I ask — does she have to be here for all of it?" Clinician: "No. Would you rather she stepped out?" R.: "Yeah." The student left and did not return.

Minute 32. R.: "What actually goes in the letter?" Clinician: "What we've talked about that your GP needs in order to help — how long this has been going on, the sleep, the weight, the drinking, what we agree to do next. Not everything you've said. And there's one thing I can't leave to you: if I thought you were in immediate danger, or someone else was, I'd have to act on that, and I'd tell you I was doing it."

Minute 45. R.: "Does the drinking have to be in it?" Clinician: "Yes, because it's tangled up with the sleep and it changes what's worth trying. I'll write what you told me and not more than that."

Definition
id definition-informed-consentlabel Informed consent

Informed consent is a person's voluntary agreement to something proposed, given with enough information to make the choice mean something, by a person able to make it. It is a continuing arrangement rather than an event. A signature or a note records that the discussion happened at a particular moment and is evidence of the agreement, not the agreement itself.

Worked Example
id worked-example-consent-as-arrangement

Task. Decide what R. had agreed to after each exchange, identify where the agreement changed, and say which change would have been impossible under a different setup.

What is given. Five exchanges, four of them timed. R. is an adult, referred, attending voluntarily. The service is a clinic; the letter goes to one GP. What is not given: the jurisdiction, the clinic's policy on student observation, and whether the waiting-area question was documented anywhere.

Principle selected. Treat the agreement as a process with a state that changes, and read each exchange for three things: what was disclosed, whether the agreement was free, and what the person could still change afterwards. That is the model Canadian professional guidance on consent to psychiatric treatment sets out. Consent is described there as a process rather than an instant, to be reviewed, revised, and renewed as circumstances change, with the form or note as the record of a moment and not the consent itself. The same guidance holds that consent does not bind the person to proceed and does not remove their right to withdraw at any time.

Plan. Take the exchanges in order, treating minutes 32 and 45 as one move made twice. For each: name what was agreed, name what was disclosed to support it, and mark whether the agreement was free. Then look for the point where the state changed, and test it by altering one feature of the setup.

Execution.

Waiting area. R. agreed to a student being present. Disclosure: that a student existed. Not disclosed: who the student was, what she was there to do, whether she would ask questions, or whether declining would affect anything. Freedom: weak. R. was standing, in outdoor clothes, in front of the person being agreed to, seconds before an appointment R. had waited weeks for. The Canadian guidance lists institutional constraints, fear, and undue influence among the circumstances that compromise voluntariness, and a waiting-area question put in front of the observer carries at least the third. That the answer was yes tells you very little.

Minute 0. The clinician disclosed their own role, the student's role, the purpose of the appointment, what would be written and to whom together with R.'s freedom to read and query it, and that R. could decline any question. Requirements for informed consent to treatment include the nature and purpose of what is proposed, its likely benefits and probable risks, the alternatives, the consequences of declining, and the identity of the person providing it. The minute-0 statement covers purpose, identity, and consequences of declining. It does not cover risks or alternatives, which is defensible here because nothing has yet been proposed to consent to. The agreement at minute 0 is an agreement to have the conversation.

Minute 24. The state changed. R. withdrew the waiting-area yes. The clinician's answer did two things at once: it confirmed the withdrawal was available, and it made no request for a reason. Compare a plausible alternative reply, "she's only got two more weeks on this placement" — accurate, unremarkable, and enough to convert a withdrawable agreement into one that costs something to withdraw.

Minutes 32 and 45. R. tested the record twice, once in general and once on a specific item. The clinician answered specifically both times and, at minute 32, named the one limit that R. does not control. Notice what that disclosure is not: it is not "everything you say is confidential", and it is not a recitation of law. It states a boundary, in one sentence, in advance.

Boundary conditions. This reading assumes R. can make these decisions. Capacity is decision-specific and is assessed against a particular choice at a particular time: the ability to understand the relevant information and to appreciate what following or refusing would mean. A psychiatric condition does not by itself establish incapacity, and neither does disagreeing with the clinician or making a choice the clinician thinks unwise. Nothing in R.'s record raises the question, and this lesson does not teach how it is assessed.

Independent check. Remove the minute-0 statement and keep everything else. R. still tests the record at minute 32, but now for the first time, 32 minutes into a conversation, after the sleep and the weight and the friends. Everything R. said before minute 32 was said without knowing where it was going. R. cannot retrieve those 32 minutes, so the only available correction is to say less from here on. The minute-0 statement costs about forty seconds and buys the rest of the appointment.

Interpretation. By the end, R. has agreed to a conversation, agreed and then unagreed to an observer, and agreed to a specific description of that conversation going to one named reader with one stated exception. There is no document anywhere that says any of that. The agreement is real and the record of it is thin, which is the ordinary situation and the reason the discussion has to be deliberate.

Self-explanation. Of the five exchanges, one made the rest possible. Which, and what exactly did it supply that the others drew on?

The minute-0 statement is the answer. It established that R. could decline things, which is what R. then did at minute 24, and it named the record as something open to discussion, which is what R. then used at minutes 32 and 45. R. did not have to work out that any of this was permitted; it had already been said.

The waiting-area question is worth one more look, because it is the version the survey numbers describe: asked about, and not introduced. In the Portuguese survey, 75% of psychiatry patients who recalled the encounter said the doctor had asked whether they minded students being present, while 31% said the students had introduced themselves as medical students and asked permission. R.'s waiting-area yes sits in the 75% and outside the 31%: R. was asked, and did not know who was being agreed to. That is exactly the gap that made the yes worth so little, and exactly the gap the minute-0 introduction closed.

The account of consent as a continuing process, the list of what has to be disclosed, the right to withdraw, the circumstances that compromise voluntariness, and the decision-specific account of capacity all come from a Canadian Psychiatric Association position paper on consent to psychiatric treatment, which sets out Canadian law and states that requirements differ between provinces. The claim that a clinician cannot promise unlimited confidentiality, and that the limits differ by place, rests on a United States review of reporting duties; the minute-32 sentence in the exchange is written as one clinician's plain statement of a limit and is not a legal formula for any jurisdiction. The student-presence figures come from one Portuguese university hospital in 2023. The exchange itself, R., the clinic, and the student are invented for this lesson.

scenes.title: Two models of consent that fail quietly
scenes.contentHtml:
Two models of consent that fail quietly

Both of the models below are held by competent people, both produce encounters that look correct from outside, and both fail in ways that leave no complaint and no incident report. That is why they need a scene of their own.

Check
id check-predict-the-failure

Commit to an answer before reading on. A clinic runs its first appointments like this: the referral letter is read out, the patient signs a one-page form headed "Consent to assessment and information sharing", and the interview begins. The form is complete, dated, countersigned, and filed.

  1. Name one thing this clinic will find out later than R.'s clinic did.
  2. Name one thing a patient here can do that R. could do, and one thing they cannot.

The first model: consent is the thing that was obtained at the start

Misconception
id misconception-consent-as-event

The model. Consent is a discrete act. It happens near the beginning, it is recorded, and afterwards it is a fact about the encounter. Questions such as "was consent obtained?" have a yes or no answer, and the file settles them.

Why it is held. It is administratively true. Services audit whether the form exists, forms are countable, and a completed form is genuine evidence that a conversation happened at a moment.

What it cannot explain. It cannot explain minute 24. R. agreed to the student in the waiting area and reversed that agreement twenty-four minutes later. Under the event model, the reversal is either a nullity, because consent was already obtained, or an anomaly to be managed. Under the process model, it is the arrangement working as intended. The event model also cannot explain why R. asked at minute 32 what goes in the letter. If consent were settled at the start, that question would be closed; it was not closed, because R. had learned by then what there was to ask about.

The better model. Consent is a continuing arrangement, reviewed and renewed as the situation changes. The written record is evidence of the discussion at a moment and does not constitute the agreement. The person's right to withdraw survives the signature, and the state of the agreement at any time is what was last discussed and not what was first written.

Where the event model comes from. Partly from law, and law differs. Some Canadian provinces have legislated consent requirements that codify the common-law position while others have not, and Quebec's civil law provides different procedures again; a clinician is expected to know the requirements of the province or territory where they work. A form built to satisfy one of those regimes is a real legal instrument. It still is not the agreement, and a service that treats the two as the same has confused a filing requirement with a conversation.

Comparing the two on R.'s case. Ask both models the same question at minute 30: what has R. agreed to? The event model says: assessment and information sharing, as per the signed form. The process model says: to have this conversation, with the student out of the room since minute 24, with a letter going to one GP that R. may read, and with one stated exception R. does not control. Only one of those two answers is usable by the person who has to write the letter that evening.

The failure is quiet because both clinics produce a completed assessment and a filed record. The difference shows up in what the second clinic never hears, and an absence does not audit.

The second model: presence is not participation

Misconception
id misconception-observer-is-neutral

The model. A learner who watches without speaking has not done anything to the patient, so the arrangements that govern doing things do not apply. Introductions are a courtesy; consent belongs to the examination and the treatment.

Why it is held. It follows from a reasonable premise. Consent attaches to interventions, and watching is not an intervention.

What it cannot explain. It cannot explain why patients behave differently when someone is watching. In the Portuguese survey, some psychiatry patients reported that a student's presence made talking about an intimate problem harder. That is a change in what the encounter produces, caused by a person who did nothing. If the observer changes the data, treating the observer as outside the arrangement puts the change beyond anyone's control.

The better model. Presence is part of the setting, so it is arranged like the rest of the setting: the person is introduced by name and role, the patient is asked in conditions where declining is easy, and the answer can be revised at any point without a reason. Where the encounter is being observed for teaching, the patient is entitled to know what the observer is there to learn.

The contested part, stated as contested. Whether a general consent signed at admission covers a student observer is genuinely disputed. A United States emergency-medicine review from 2006 records that many institutions treat the admission consent as sufficient while other writers hold that explicit consent should be sought for each observation, and states separately that visitors should be present only with the patient's permission. This lesson does not resolve that. It observes that the two readings produce different encounters and that a learner should know which one their institution uses before relying on either.

Recheck in a new case. A student sits in on a consultation, says nothing, and afterwards writes a reflective account for a portfolio, changing the patient's name. Did anything happen that the patient should have been asked about? Answer from the acts: someone was present who altered the conditions of disclosure, and a written account of a private conversation now exists in a second place with a second reader. Both are arrangements. Neither is an intervention.

The related error about role

The third failure follows from the second and is worth naming because it is the one a learner in this course is most likely to make. It is the belief that the boundary between studying psychiatry and practising it is drawn around subject matter, so that reading about suicide risk is bold, discussing it is bolder, and asking someone about it is the natural next step.

The boundary is drawn around acts and the people they land on. Reading R.'s record and arguing about which arrangement produced which fact is study, and it can go as deep as you can take it. Asking a real person a direct question about suicidal thoughts is an act with a person on the other end of it, and whoever asks has committed themselves to what happens next: to hearing the answer, to knowing what to do with it, and to being the person who was there. The evidence that asking does not plant the thought removes one objection to a clinician doing it. It supplies nobody with the clinical authority, the supervision, or the route onwards that doing it requires. That term keeps the meaning Welcome to Psychiatry (PSY-WEL-001) gave it: the jurisdiction-dependent responsibility and authorisation to act clinically with real people, which academic knowledge alone does not create.

Callout
id callout-teaching-boundary-misconception

Teaching example, not medical advice. The clinic in the prediction task, the portfolio case, and R. are invented. Nothing here describes what any real service must do, and the legal position on observers, records, and confidentiality differs by jurisdiction and by institution.

Feedback on the prediction task

The signed-form clinic will find out later, or not at all, what its patients did not want written down. The form names information sharing in general and settles it; R.'s clinic named one reader and one exception and left the question open, which is why R. raised it twice. A patient at the signed-form clinic can still decline a question, because that right does not depend on being told about it. What they cannot easily do is revise something already agreed, because the arrangement has been recorded as complete and reopening it means contradicting a document with their own signature on it.

scenes.title: Three passes, with the scaffolding taken away
scenes.contentHtml:
Three passes, with the scaffolding taken away

Work each pass before opening its feedback. The first supplies the procedure, the second supplies only the question, and the third supplies neither.

First pass: change one thing, find the consequence

The procedure has three steps. Name the setup decision that changed. Name what R. could no longer do, or could now do, as a result. Then name the specific line in the record that appears, disappears, or arrives at a different time.

Check
id check-alter-the-setup

For each change, run the three steps. Keep everything else about R.'s appointment as it was.

  1. The appointment is 15 minutes instead of 50.
  2. The student stays for the whole appointment and nobody offers R. a way to change that.
  3. Nothing is said at minute 0 about the letter to the GP.
  4. R.'s partner, who drove R. to the clinic, is invited in to help because R. seems tired.

Feedback after your attempt

  1. The decision is time. At 15 minutes the order of questions becomes the whole of the interview, because the end arrives before the list does. In R.'s appointment the alcohol came at minute 34 and the direct question at minute 40; neither survives a 15-minute slot unless something else is dropped. Fifteen minutes is not an unrealistic figure: across 67 countries, average primary-care consultation length ran from 48 seconds to 22.5 minutes, and 18 countries holding about half the world's population sat at five minutes or less.
  2. The decision is people, and the missing piece is the offer to change it. R. can still decline questions, so the likely effect is a shorter, flatter answer to whichever question R. would have preferred the student not to hear, and outright silence is the less likely outcome. In the Portuguese survey, some psychiatry patients reported that a student's presence made an intimate problem harder to discuss. The line that changes is the one about the friends R. has stopped seeing, or the one about the drinking, and you cannot tell which from the record afterwards.
  3. The decision is the record. Everything R. says now travels to an unnamed destination. More than half of the respondents in two United States surveys who withheld something from a clinician named keeping it out of the medical record as a reason. R.'s two questions at minutes 32 and 45 do not disappear; they move later, or they turn into a shorter answer where the question would have been.
  4. The decision is people, dressed up as communication access. A partner brought in to help is a third person in the room, and a companion is not one of the arrangements that communication access means. A systematic review found professional interpreters associated with fewer errors and better comprehension, outcomes, and satisfaction than family members and other ad hoc interpreters, and the same objection applies with more force to a topic the person may not want the accompanying adult to hear. If R. is tired, the arrangement to make is a second appointment at a different time of day.

Second pass: start from the record, find the decision

Now the procedure is gone and only the question remains. Each line below is written as it might appear in R.'s record. For each, name the setup decision that produced it.

Check
id check-infer-the-decision
  1. "Declined to answer further questions about family history."
  2. "Patient became tearful; interview concluded shortly afterwards."
  3. "Alcohol intake not established."
  4. "Patient asked who else would see the letter."
  5. "Collateral history not available at this appointment."

Feedback after your attempt

  1. Someone told R. that declining was available, and R. used it. Absent that, the same silence appears in the record as a fuller answer given reluctantly, or as nothing at all.
  2. Two candidates, and the record does not distinguish them. Either the appointment ended because it was finished, or it ended because the slot did. Which one it was is a fact about the setting, and whoever wrote the line knew it and did not write it down.
  3. The item was reached and the answer was unclear, or the item was never reached. The second is a time decision and the first is not, and again the record does not say. A record that reported the minute at which the interview ended would settle it.
  4. R. knew that a letter existed, so someone said so at the start. The question also tells you R. is thinking about readers beyond the one who was named, which the opening statement did not settle.
  5. Nobody arranged for one. Whether a family member or a GP could add anything is a question that has to be raised, and consented to, before the appointment and not during it.

Third pass: no support at all

Check
id check-rebuild-the-encounter

An invented case, unconnected to R. A community team offers a first appointment to a 27-year-old referred after two visits to an emergency department. As arranged, it runs like this: the appointment is in a shared open-plan assessment area with screens between bays; two team members attend, neither introduced by role; the slot is 20 minutes and a third of it is spent on a laptop entering details; the person's mother is in the bay because she brought them; the person is asked to sign a form headed "consent to assessment" without it being read out; nothing is said about who receives a summary.

Do three things.

  1. Rewrite the arrangements. Change only the setup, and for each change say what it buys.
  2. Two of the original arrangements are defensible under some conditions. Identify them and state the conditions.
  3. Name two facts that the rebuilt encounter could produce and the original could not, and say why each one specifically depends on the change you made.

Feedback after your attempt

A strong answer changes at least these: a room where the conversation cannot be overheard; both team members introduced by name and role, with the second's reason for attending stated; the mother asked to wait outside for at least part of the appointment, with the person asked in private whether she should return; the laptop either used openly with the screen visible or set aside; a spoken account at the start of what will be written and who will read it, including the limits; and either a longer slot or an explicit statement of what a 20-minute appointment will and will not cover.

The two defensible arrangements are the second team member and the short slot. A second attender is defensible when the person has been told who they are and why they are there, and it is sometimes required, for example where a service's own safety policy calls for two staff. A 20-minute slot is defensible when it is named as a first of several and when what it is for is stated, so that the person is not left believing that everything had to fit.

For the third part, the two facts should each hang on one change. Anything the person did not want the mother to hear depends on the mother leaving, and no other change substitutes for it. Anything the person is only willing to say once they know where it goes depends on the account of the record, which is the reason more than half of the people in those United States surveys who withheld something gave for withholding it. A weaker answer names two facts and attributes both to a general improvement in atmosphere.

Where to go next

  • All three passes clean: continue to the telephone follow-up.
  • Trouble in the first pass: you are probably naming the effect on the clinician's workload instead of the effect on what the person can say. Redo item 2 and write only sentences whose subject is R.
  • Trouble in the second pass: for each item, write down the two setups that would produce the identical line, then say what would have to be added to the record to tell them apart.
  • Trouble in the third pass: rebuild it as a list of the six decisions from the second scene, with the original in one column and yours in the other. If a row is empty, that decision was never made in either version.

Recovery route

If sorting observation from report from addition in the first scene was where you came unstuck, that is the preceding outcome, Description, inference, and interpretation, and this lesson leans on it without teaching it. You can rebuild enough of it here: take any three sentences from a record and, for each, write who would have to be asked to check it. If the answer is the patient, it is a report. If the answer is anyone who was in the room, it is an observation. If there is nobody to ask, someone added it.

If the consent material read as familiar and you found the practice harder than expected, the gap is usually that consent is being held as a topic rather than as a state that changes. Take R.'s five exchanges and write the state after each one as a single sentence beginning "R. has agreed to". Five sentences. If any two are identical, look again at what changed.

If the role boundary is still doing the work of a warning instead of a test, apply the table from the second scene to three tasks you might plausibly do this week. For each, name who it lands on and what follows if you are wrong. The topic is not part of the test and should not appear in your answer.

If the six decisions do not come back from memory, do not reread the scene first. Write the list, then check it, then write the consequence each one had in R.'s appointment. Checking before retrieving is the one order that will not help.

scenes.title: The same six decisions, by telephone
scenes.contentHtml:
The same six decisions, by telephone

Two weeks later R. has a 15-minute telephone review. R. takes it in the warehouse car park at 9.40pm, twenty minutes before a night shift, with a partner in the passenger seat. The clinician has a phone, a screen, and no idea of any of that.

Everything arranged for the first appointment has to be arranged again, and three of the six decisions now behave differently. The point of this scene is that the six decisions are the transferable part and the specific arrangements are not; a rule learned as "check the room, introduce the student" transfers to nothing.

What the telephone takes away

Place becomes unverifiable. In the consulting room, the clinician could see the door. On the phone, the only route to that information is to ask, and the question has to be asked in a form that a person sitting next to someone can answer safely. "Are you somewhere you can talk?" can be answered yes by a person who is not, without lying, because a car with the window up is somewhere you can talk. "Is there anyone with you?" is answerable with a single word in front of that person and cannot be. Whichever question is asked, the clinician has to expect the answer to be shaped by whoever can hear it, and to read a shorter conversation as evidence about the setting and not as evidence about R.

People becomes invisible, and identity becomes a question. In the room, the clinician knew who R. was because R. was sitting there. On the phone the clinician has a voice and a number, and the person who answers a number is not necessarily the person the number belongs to. That check has no counterpart in the first appointment.

Time is set by the person who has the shift. Fifteen minutes was the clinic's figure; 9.40pm and a 10pm start are R.'s. The clinician has a slot and R. has a hard stop, and only one of them knows it. If nobody asks how long R. has, the call will end in the middle of something and the record will say the review was completed.

What stays the same, and is easier to forget

The agreement from two weeks ago does not carry over by itself. R. agreed to a conversation in a room, and consent is renewed as the circumstances change; the last occasion does not supply it. A phone call from a car park with someone else present is a changed circumstance in every respect that matters, and the right to stop it is the same right R. used at minute 24 of the first appointment.

The record question returns in a new form. R. now knows that a letter goes to the GP and knows the exception. What R. does not know is whether this call is being recorded, whether a summary of it joins the same file, and whether anyone else has read the first letter since. More than half of the respondents in two United States surveys who withheld information from a clinician gave keeping it out of the medical record as a reason, and R. has already shown, twice, that this is a live question for R. specifically.

Check
id check-transfer-telephone

Arrange this call. Write it as a short numbered list of what you would establish, in the order you would establish it, before asking anything about the past two weeks.

Then answer three questions about your own arrangement.

  1. Which item on your list has no counterpart in the first appointment, and why does the telephone create it?
  2. R. answers "yeah, fine" to your privacy question in a tone you would describe as flat. Name two different setups that produce that answer and say what you would do differently under each.
  3. The call is going to run past 10pm. Name what you would give up and say why that item and not another.

Feedback after your attempt

A workable order establishes, first, who is on the phone; then how long R. has, in R.'s numbers and not the clinic's; then whether R. can speak freely where R. is and whether someone else can hear; then whether this call joins the same record and who reads it; then that R. can stop, reschedule, or decline any part without giving a reason. Only after all five does the review begin.

The item with no counterpart is identity. In the room it was settled by R. being in it. This is the clearest sign that the six decisions are the durable thing: the decision "establish who is here" survives into the new setting, while the arrangement that satisfied it does not.

A flat "yeah, fine" is produced by at least two setups: R. is alone and tired at the end of a bad fortnight, or R. is not alone and cannot say so. The two call for different responses, and the useful move is one that works under both without requiring you to know which. Offering a closed question that a person can answer safely in company, and offering a different time, costs little if R. is simply tired and matters a great deal if R. is not alone.

For the time question, the answer that transfers is to give up whatever can be done in writing or at a later appointment and keep whatever depends on this conversation happening now. What must not be given up is the ending: a call cut off by a shift leaves R. in a car park at 10pm holding the last minutes of a mental-health conversation with nowhere to put them.

Callout
id callout-teaching-boundary-transfer

Teaching example, not medical advice. The telephone review is invented. This scene teaches how to read an arrangement, and it does not describe how any service should conduct remote appointments, which is governed by local policy, professional regulation, and law.

Accessibility and alternatives

Every task in this lesson can be answered in prose, in a list, or in a table, and typed, dictated, handwritten, or given aloud to a tutor. Nothing is timed and nothing depends on colour, position on a page, sound, motion, dragging, or a hover. The lesson contains two tables and no images, diagrams, charts, audio, or video. Each table row carries its own reasoning in words and reads as an ordinary sentence when the columns are taken in order, so a reader working through the text in a single column loses nothing. No task asks about your own health, treatment, or experience, and none requires you to disclose anything about yourself.

This lesson describes suicidal thoughts in one fictional person and discusses what makes them easier or harder to talk about. If that is difficult reading today, stop, and come back or do not; nothing here is assessed on speed and nothing is monitored. EmbeddedKnowledge is a set of documents and provides no care of any kind. For personal help, use a qualified local service or your area's current emergency route.

The proportion of people who named the medical record as a reason for withholding comes from two United States survey samples and describes what respondents said about themselves. scenes.title: Clinical wrap-up: one sentence in a letter to a GP
scenes.contentHtml:
Clinical wrap-up: one sentence in a letter to a GP

Callout
id callout-teaching-boundary-wrap-up

Teaching example, not medical advice. R., the clinic, the appointment, and the letter are invented for this course. This scene works through a documentation and consent question and gives no guidance on assessing or responding to suicide risk, which belongs to a later outcome and to supervised clinical training. Nothing here tells any clinician what to write, and nothing here is a basis for any decision about any real person.

The appointment ended at 4.50pm. The letter to R.'s GP has to be written this evening, and the clinic has a template with headings for history, examination, impression, and plan. Everything in it is straightforward except one sentence. Does the line about passive thoughts that life is not worth the effort go into the letter?

This is a real clinical question with a real consequence for the person receiving the letter. It is also, and this is the point of the scene, a question that was mostly answered at minute 0.

Work it with the lesson's own tools

What did R. agree to? Three statements, taken together. At minute 0: a letter would go to the GP, R. could read it, and R. could ask for anything in it to be discussed first. At minute 32: it would carry what the GP needs in order to help, and not everything R. said. At minute 45: R. asked about a specific item, was told yes, and was told why. R. therefore agreed to a described letter with a named reader, and R. agreed to it knowing that some things would be in it that R. had not chosen.

Does the stated exception apply? At minute 32 the clinician named the one thing not left to R.: immediate danger, and the promise to say so if it were being acted on. That exception governs a situation this letter does not describe. What is in the record is passive thought without plan, intent, or act. Writing to a GP as part of ordinary care is not the exception being invoked. Reaching for it here would use a rule meant for an emergency to settle a routine question about a letter, and a rule used that way stops meaning anything on the day it is needed.

Who reads this, and can R.? One named GP, plus whoever at that practice has access to the record. R. can read it, because R. was told so. That fact changes the writing. When patients at three German psychiatric outpatient clinics gained online access to their notes, documentation changed measurably: across 876 notes before and after, stigmatising, controlling, and incomprehensible language fell and comprehensible, personal, and resource-oriented language rose. The clinicians interviewed said the substance of what they documented was unchanged and described handling sensitive material through more general phrasing. That study covers three German outpatient clinics and compares two periods with no control site, so it does not establish that access causes the change. It does describe what changed where access arrived, and the shape of it is worth having: the readable version differed in how things were written far more than in whether they were there.

What does each option cost?

Option What the GP can do What it does to the next conversation
Leave the sentence out Reviews R. without knowing there is anything to review against. Any later change has no baseline. Nothing, until R. reads the letter and finds that the one thing hardest to say is the one thing missing.
Put it in without telling R. Has what it needs. R. reads a sentence R. did not know was going in. R. now has direct evidence that what is said in the room turns up in writing unannounced.
Put it in, having said in the room that it would be there Has what it needs. R. reads a letter that matches what R. was told. Nothing has to be repaired.

The third option is the only one that costs nothing later, and it is only available if something was said earlier. That is the whole argument of this lesson in one row of a table. More than half of the people in two United States surveys who withheld something from a clinician named keeping it out of the medical record as a reason; the second option manufactures exactly that reason for R., and it does so at the moment R. has most to lose by acting on it.

So what does the clinician do this evening? Writes the sentence, in the terms R. used, in the section where a GP will find it, because the letter was described to R. as carrying what the GP needs. And the reason the clinician can do that without a phone call to R. first is that R. was told, in the room, what the letter was for and that R. could read it and query it. Had that not been said, the honest options this evening would be a call to R. or an incomplete letter, and both are more expensive than forty seconds at minute 0.

What you should be able to reconstruct

Close this and answer from memory.

  1. The six decisions, in any order, with the consequence each one had in R.'s appointment.
  2. What changed about R.'s agreement at minute 24, and what made that change available.
  3. One thing a person in a non-clinical role may do with this material and one thing they may not, justified from the act and not from the topic.
  4. Why "was consent obtained?" is the wrong shape of question, and what to ask instead.

For the fourth: ask what the person has agreed to now, what they were told in order to agree to it, and what they can still change. A yes-or-no question about the past has no answer that is useful this evening.

Where this goes next

The outcome that follows this one, open and focused inquiry, takes the arranged conversation and asks how the questions inside it are put. Mental-status observation, later in the same module, describes R.'s state without turning the description into a verdict, and it will keep running into this lesson: what a person shows you is partly a fact about the room they are showing it in. Further on, the mood outcomes ask what R.'s picture might be, and the alcohol, the weight, an episode six years ago that nobody assessed, and a blood test nobody has done all come back. Each of those facts is in the record because of a decision made before R. spoke, and none of them is more secure than the arrangement that produced it.

assessment.title: Setting, role, and consent mastery check

items.prompt: Take each of the four lines from the record in turn. For each, name the setup decision that most plausibly produced it, say what the line would have looked like under the alternative given beside it, and say what a reader of the record cannot tell from the line as written. Then name the one line that could have been produced by two different setups, and state what would have to be added to the record to tell them apart.
items.stimulus:
An invented first-appointment record for a fictional adult, unconnected to R.

1. "Attended alone. Declined to discuss family history today." Alternative: the person's brother was in the room throughout.
2. "Sleep, appetite and mood covered. Alcohol not discussed." Alternative: the appointment was 45 minutes rather than 15.
3. "Asked whether the summary would go to her employer." Alternative: nothing was said at the start about who receives the summary.
4. "Answered questions in short sentences, appeared guarded." Alternative: the room was a curtained bay in a shared assessment area.

answer.correct: Line 1 turns on people: attending alone made declining available in a way it is not with a relative present, and under the alternative the same silence would appear as a fuller but edited answer or as agreement with the brother's account. Line 2 turns on time: a 15-minute slot ends before the list does, so the alternative most likely produces a recorded alcohol history rather than its absence. Line 3 turns on the record: the question exists because someone named a reader, and under the alternative the person either does not ask at all or asks much later, having already spoken without knowing where it went. Line 4 turns on place: guardedness recorded in a curtained bay is at least partly a description of the bay, and the alternative makes the line evidence about the setting as much as about the person. Line 4 is the ambiguous one, and separating a person's manner from the conditions it was shown in requires the record to state where the conversation happened and whether it could be overheard. A strong answer also notes for lines 1 and 2 that the record cannot distinguish a topic declined from a topic never reached.
answer.summary: Each line is traced to a specific decision, the alternative changes a specific line, and the ambiguous line is identified with the missing information named.
answer.reasoning: The outcome requires treating the arrangements as part of the clinical material. A response that attributes every line to the person's characteristics has missed the target; so has one that attributes every line to the setting, since line 3 shows a setup decision producing information rather than suppressing it. The demand to say what a reader cannot tell is what separates tracing from guessing: the record supports a range of setups, and naming the missing detail is the honest end of the analysis.
acceptableResponses: Line 4 may be attributed to people rather than place if the response argues that a shared bay implies audible neighbours, provided the missing information named is still about the conditions of the conversation.
Line 2 may be attributed jointly to time and to the order of questions, since the order is itself a consequence of the time available.
A response may name line 1 rather than line 4 as the ambiguous one if it identifies the same missing information, namely whether the topic was reached at all.
commonErrors: Explaining every line by the person's mood, personality, or willingness rather than by an arrangement.
Treating the alternative as making the encounter generally better or worse instead of changing one identified line.
Reading 'appeared guarded' as an observation when it is a listener's addition.
Naming a decision without saying what it did, for example writing 'time' with no consequence attached.

items.prompt: Select every statement that correctly describes R.'s agreement at minute 46 of the first appointment.
items.stimulus: R. agreed in the waiting area to a medical student being present. At minute 0 the clinician stated their own role, the student's role, the purpose of the appointment, that a letter would go to the GP which R. could read and query, and that R. could decline any question. At minute 24 R. asked the student to leave and she did. At minute 32 R. asked what the letter would contain and was told, including one exception the clinician would act on. At minute 45 R. asked about a specific item and was told it would be included and why.

options.text: What R. has agreed to is what was last discussed, which includes the student being absent since minute 24.
The waiting-area agreement to the student still stands, because it was given first and was never formally revoked.
R. has agreed to a described letter going to one named reader, and not to unrestricted sharing.
R. can still change any part of this, including asking at minute 50 that something discussed earlier be left out.
Because nothing was signed, no consent exists and the clinician should obtain one before writing anything.

answer.summary: The agreement is a current state that includes the minute-24 revision, covers a described letter to one reader, and remains open to change.
answer.reasoning: Consent here is a state that the last discussion sets, so the waiting-area answer was superseded at minute 24 and does not survive as a standing permission. The letter was described rather than authorised in general, which is why R. could usefully ask about a specific item at minute 45. The right to change what has been agreed is not spent by having agreed, so the fourth statement holds even at minute 50. The final option inverts the relationship between the agreement and its record: the absence of a signature means the record of the discussion is thin, and it does not mean the discussion did not happen or that the agreement is void.
commonErrors: Treating the earliest agreement as the authoritative one because it came first.
Reading a described letter as general permission to share.
Assuming a signature is what makes an agreement real.
Assuming that once a topic has been discussed the person can no longer ask for it to be handled differently.

items.prompt: A learner working through this course wants to do one of the following this week. Which one stays inside a non-clinical role, and for the reason given?

options.text: Rewrite the arrangements of the invented 20-minute encounter from the practice scene and defend each change, because the object is a fictional record and being wrong changes an argument.
Ask a friend who has seemed low the direct question the lesson showed being asked, because the evidence in this lesson indicates that asking does not create the thought.
Tell a relative what their local clinic will and will not put in a letter, because this lesson explained how such letters are decided.
Avoid the practice items that mention suicidal thoughts, because a learner without clinical authority should not study that subject at all.

answer.summary: Rewriting a fictional setup is study; the other three either act on a real person or misplace the boundary around the topic.
answer.reasoning: The boundary follows the act and the person it lands on. Rewriting an invented encounter produces an inspectable argument and lands on nobody. Asking a friend the direct question lands on a real person and commits whoever asks to what follows, and evidence that asking does not plant the thought removes an objection without supplying authorisation, supervision, or a route onwards. Telling a relative what a clinic will write is a statement about a real service's practice and its jurisdiction's law, made without standing to know either. The fourth option makes the opposite error: it draws the boundary around the subject matter, which would rule out studying the material at all and is exactly the confusion the lesson repairs.
commonErrors: Choosing the friend option because the lesson's evidence about asking is read as permission.
Choosing the relative option because the information seems helpful and no assessment is involved.
Choosing avoidance because the topic feels like the thing that needs authority.

items.prompt: Arrange this encounter. Write what you would establish and in what order, before any clinical question is asked. Then do four things: state which of the six decisions the video format changes and how; state what the person has agreed to once your arrangement is complete, in one sentence beginning 'They have agreed to'; name one thing you would say about the record and one limit you would name; and identify one act in your plan that a learner in a non-clinical role could not perform and say why, arguing from the act rather than from the subject matter.
items.stimulus: An invented case. A service offers a 30-minute video appointment to a fictional 41-year-old who has been on a waiting list for five months and joins from a shared house on a phone propped against a laptop. A trainee will be observing on the call. The consultation will be recorded for the trainee's supervision.

answer.correct: A workable order establishes who is on the call and confirms identity; whether the person can speak freely where they are and whether anyone else in the house can hear; that a trainee is present, who the trainee is, and what the trainee is there for, with a real opportunity to decline that is offered before the trainee appears rather than in front of them; that the call will be recorded, who will see the recording, how long it is kept, and that recording can be declined separately from the appointment itself; how long the person has and what a 30-minute appointment will and will not cover; what will be written and who receives it, with one stated limit that is not the person's to control; and that any part of this can be changed at any point without a reason. Only then does the clinical conversation begin. The video format changes place, because the clinician sees one framed rectangle and not the room, so privacy has to be asked about and cannot be observed; people, for the same reason, since anyone outside the frame is invisible; and the record, because a recording is a second and more complete record than a note and needs its own agreement. It leaves time, role, and communication access needing the same decisions as any other setting, though the five-month wait puts pressure on the person to accept whatever is offered, which is a voluntariness problem and not a scheduling one. The agreement sentence should name the described encounter, the trainee's presence or absence, the recording or its refusal, the reader of any summary, and the stated limit. The act a learner could not perform is the clinical part: proposing or conducting the assessment itself, or making any decision that follows from what the person says. The justification must run through the act and its consequences and must not mention how difficult or sensitive the subject is.
answer.summary: Arrange the six decisions for a video appointment with an observer and a recording, state the resulting agreement in one sentence, and place the role boundary by act.
answer.reasoning: This is transfer because the setting is new in three respects the lesson did not work through: a video frame, a recording, and a long wait that pressures the answer. The six decisions still apply and the specific arrangements do not carry over, which is the transferable lesson. Recording deserves its own agreement because it creates a second record with different readers, and the withholding evidence in this lesson shows that people alter what they say according to what they believe is being kept. The five-month wait is the voluntariness point in a form the lesson did not supply: an agreement given by someone who fears losing an appointment they waited five months for is not freely given in the sense the consent model requires.
acceptableResponses: A response may argue that the trainee should be introduced at the start of the call rather than before it, provided it says how declining is made easy in that arrangement.
A response may decide that recording is declined by default and offered rather than assumed, provided the reasoning is about the second record and its readers.
The order of the establishing steps may vary as long as identity, privacy, and the observer's presence come before any clinical question.
The named limit may be stated in general terms without citing any statute, and a response that says the limit depends on the jurisdiction is stronger than one that states a rule as universal.
commonErrors: Treating the video format as a room with a camera and reusing the first appointment's arrangements unchanged.
Folding the recording into the general agreement to the appointment instead of asking about it separately.
Missing the five-month wait as a pressure on voluntariness.
Justifying the role boundary by saying the topic is too sensitive for a learner, which is the error the lesson repairs.
Writing an agreement sentence so general that it would be true of any appointment anywhere.

rubrics.title: Tracing a record back to its arrangements

criteria.description: Names a specific setup decision for each of the four lines instead of a general quality of the encounter.
States, for each line, what the alternative arrangement would have produced in the record, at the level of the line rather than of the appointment.
Says for at least two lines what a reader of the record cannot determine from the line as written.
Identifies a line that two different setups would produce and names the information the record would need in order to separate them.

rubrics.title: Reading the current state of an agreement

criteria.description: Selects the statements describing the agreement as a current state that includes the minute-24 revision, covers a described letter to a named reader, and remains open to change.
Rejects both the claim that the earliest answer still stands and the claim that an unsigned agreement is no agreement.

rubrics.title: Placing the role boundary by act

criteria.description: Selects the act whose object is a fictional record and whose failure mode is a wrong argument.
Establishes identity, privacy, the observer's presence, the recording, time, and the record before any clinical question, in a defensible order.
Says which of the six decisions the video format and the recording change, and how, instead of restating the first appointment's arrangements.

States the resulting agreement in one specific sentence and names both something about the record and a limit that is not the person's to control, without presenting any jurisdiction's rule as universal.
Identifies an act a non-clinical role could not perform and justifies it from the act and the person it lands on, with no appeal to the sensitivity of the topic.
